01 / One step at a time

What is a smart home?

Connected devices help with everyday tasks. Control them by phone or voice, or let an automation act for you.

Control

Turn off a light from your phone without leaving the sofa.

Automate

Turn on the hallway light when someone walks by.

Check

Check whether a window was left open before going out.

Start with one need, one light or one sensor. There is no need to automate the whole house.

Explore the connected home

A different atmosphere.

12 devices to explore

Zigbee

Smart bulbs

Color for atmosphere. Warm or cool white for every moment.

What to check

RGBCCT combines RGB with adjustable white color temperature. Check the features exposed by the model in ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT.

Read the guide ↗
WLED · ESPHome

LED strips

Indirect light, color and scenes that follow your day.

What to check

Addressable and analog strips need different controllers. Match strip type, voltage, power supply and controller.

Read the guide ↗
Zigbee · Wi-Fi

Smart relays

Discreet automation that keeps your existing wall switch.

What to check

Check neutral, voltage, load rating and wall-box space. Mains installation requires a qualified electrician.

Read the guide ↗
Zigbee · Wi-Fi · Matter

Smart plugs

Control appliances and, with supported models, track energy use.

What to check

Check plug type, current rating and energy metering. Matter does not guarantee every feature of the vendor app.

Read the guide ↗
mmWave · PIR

Presence sensors

Light follows room occupancy without a button press.

What to check

PIR responds to motion; mmWave radar can detect smaller movements. Position, zones and sensitivity need tuning.

Read the guide ↗
Zigbee · Thread

Door & window sensors

Know what is open and use that state in your automations.

What to check

Align both parts within the manufacturer’s specified gap. A contact detects opening; it does not confirm the door is locked.

Read the guide ↗
Zigbee · ESPHome

Temperature & humidity

Understand each room’s comfort with measurements throughout the day.

What to check

Avoid direct sunlight and heat sources. Check accuracy, update interval and calibration support.

Read the guide ↗
Dashboard · ESP32

Smart panels

Lights, climate and scenes on a screen everyone can reach.

What to check

A tablet can display a Home Assistant dashboard. ESP32 panels use their own interfaces, for example ESPHome with LVGL.

Read the guide ↗
Wi-Fi · Ethernet

Smart TVs

Bring your TV into movie scenes and living-room controls.

What to check

Integration depends on the manufacturer and model. Network power-on may need Wake-on-LAN or a standby setting.

Read the guide ↗
Echo · Assist

Alexa & voice

Voice commands for scenes and everyday tasks.

What to check

Alexa relies on online services. Nabu Casa simplifies Home Assistant integration; Assist offers alternatives, including local options.

Read the guide ↗
Zigbee · Matter · Wi-Fi

Smart locks

Check lock status and organize access to your home.

What to check

Check door fit, emergency access, batteries and model integration. Local operation varies by product.

Read the guide ↗
ESPHome · Wi-Fi

ESP32 projects

Build sensors, controls and devices around your own ideas.

What to check

Choose a supported board and components. Start with a low-voltage project and follow the ESPHome documentation.

Read the guide ↗

02 / One step at a time

Which platform brings it together?

These platforms can coexist. Here, Home Assistant is the hub; other systems can complement it.

Our guide’s focus

Home Assistant

A hub that brings devices and automations from different brands together.

Advantages
Local control, choice and flexible automations.
Limitations
Needs an always-on hub, initial setup and maintenance.
Official reference

Platform

Alexa

Amazon’s ecosystem, known for Echo devices and voice commands.

Advantages
Convenient voice control and simple routines with supported devices.
Limitations
Many features use the cloud; radios and capabilities vary by Echo model.
Official reference

Platform

Google Home

Google’s app and ecosystem for organizing and controlling your home.

Advantages
Combines controls, voice and supported Matter devices.
Limitations
Matter needs a compatible hub; remote access and online services need internet.
Official reference

Platform

Apple Home / HomeKit

The Home app connects supported accessories to iPhone and Siri.

Advantages
Fits Apple devices and Home app automations.
Limitations
Remote access and automations need an Apple home hub; check accessory support.
Official reference

Platform

Samsung SmartThings

An app for Samsung devices and other supported brands.

Advantages
Visual routines; some can run locally on a compatible hub.
Limitations
Not every routine is local. Features and protocols depend on devices and the hub.
Official reference

Platform

Tuya / Smart Life

A platform used by many brands, often through the Smart Life app.

Advantages
Easy phone-based setup and many device categories.
Limitations
Features and quality vary; many functions use the cloud, although some hubs run local scenes.
Official reference

Our learning path: Home Assistant OS with local Zigbee. An Alexa or Smart Life badge alone does not guarantee direct Home Assistant support: check the exact model.

03 / One step at a time

Home Assistant: the center of your home.

Free, open-source software that brings controls, sensors and automations onto one screen. It runs on an always-on device at home.

You use buttons and menus.

The screen shows the lights, temperatures and devices you add. Start by opening a device, naming it and assigning a room.

With local devices and integrations, automations work without internet. The hub and local network must stay on; cloud services still need internet.

Understand Home Assistant →

04 / One step at a time

Choose your home’s hub.

HAOS needs an always-on computer at home. Choose from the ready-to-use Green to more capable mini PCs.

For an easy start, choose Green. For more headroom, consider an N150 with 16 GB.

Easiest first step

Home Assistant Green

4 GB RAM · 32 GB eMMC

Advantages
HAOS preinstalled, silent and energy efficient. Just connect power and Ethernet.
Trade-offs
Fixed internal memory and storage. Less suited to camera recording and demanding tasks.
Price checkCheck with suppliersConfirm shipping and import taxes.

For hands-on beginners

Raspberry Pi 5

8 GB RAM · SSD NVMe 500 GB / 1 TB

Advantages
Compact, well documented and capable of home automation. An SSD provides more space and write endurance than a basic memory card.
Trade-offs
Add a suitable power supply, cooling, case and M.2 HAT adapter. Assembly and NVMe boot need preparation; a full kit can cost as much as a mini PC.
Price checkGet a full kit quoteBoard, SSD, case, cooling, power supply and M.2 adapter.

A balanced HAOS choice

Mini-PC Intel N150

16 GB RAM · 500 GB or 1 TB SSD/NVMe

Advantages
Balances performance, size and power use. Has room for HAOS, ZHA and several Apps.
Trade-offs
Requires HAOS installation. Choose 32 GB only when the PC manufacturer confirms support: Intel specifies up to 16 GB.
Price checkCheck availability and priceNTC 14N150-1103 · 16 GB / 512 GB · listing sold out with no price on 21 October 2026.

Room to grow

Mini-PC Ryzen 5

16 or 32 GB RAM · 500 GB or 1 TB SSD/NVMe

Advantages
Headroom for more Apps and simultaneous tasks. Many models allow RAM and SSD upgrades.
Trade-offs
May use more power and have an audible fan. CPU generation matters: not every Ryzen 5 is recent or upgradeable.
Price checkCheck the model’s priceChoose the model and confirm CPU, RAM and SSD.

For more demanding plans

Mini-PC Ryzen 7

16 or 32 GB RAM · 500 GB or 1 TB SSD/NVMe

Advantages
Recent models offer plenty of performance to grow into. Makes sense when you already have specific plans for demanding workloads.
Trade-offs
Higher cost and more performance than basic ZHA needs. Power use, heat and noise vary widely by model.
Price checkSee offers by modelK6 and K8 Plus have different configurations and prices; see the sources below.

Keep it simple

You don’t need the fastest one.

16 GB and 500/512 GB provide plenty of room for a first mini PC. 32 GB and 1 TB are expansion options, not HAOS requirements.

For all these options, budget separately for ZBT-2 for our Zigbee network. Use Ethernet and keep backups outside the hub.

For mini PCs, check UEFI and network compatibility. Installing HAOS directly on the disk erases the existing system.

06 / One step at a time

Zigbee: our first network.

Zigbee is a wireless connection for lights, buttons and sensors. It uses its own network rather than adding every device to Wi-Fi.

Why start with Zigbee?

A wide device selection, low-power battery sensors and local control through ZHA. Suitable mains-powered devices can relay the signal.

What to check

Needs a coordinator such as ZBT-2. Walls and 2.4 GHz interference affect reception. Battery sensors usually do not relay signals; check each model’s support.

What about Thread?

Another low-power network, often used by Matter devices. It connects through a Thread border router. Useful, but it adds that requirement and needs compatibility checks.

ZBT-2 uses Zigbee or Thread, one at a time. This path keeps it on Zigbee.

Understand Zigbee →

07 / One step at a time

Matter: a shared language for brands.

Matter is a standard for connecting supported devices to different platforms. It can use Wi-Fi, Ethernet or Thread. Matter and Thread are different things.

Benefit: it can make one device available to multiple ecosystems. Limitation: feature support varies; Matter-over-Thread devices need a Thread border router and a Matter controller. You can start with Zigbee and explore Matter later.

Understand Matter and Thread (PT) →

08 / One step at a time

ZBT-2 + ZHA: connect your first device.

ZBT-2 is the USB adapter that speaks Zigbee. ZHA is Home Assistant’s built-in integration for managing that network.

  1. Connect ZBT-2 to the hub with its USB cable, away from your router and metal objects.
  2. Under Settings → Devices & services, add the discovered ZBT-2.
  3. Choose “Use as Zigbee adapter” and “Recommended installation”. The wizard sets up ZHA.
  4. In ZHA, choose Add device, then put your light or sensor into pairing mode following its manual.
See the illustrated steps →

Zigbee2MQTT (Z2M) is another option, covered in further learning (PT).

09 / One step at a time

Your first automation, without code.

Let’s switch on a light at sunset. Choose what starts the automation and what it does.

  1. Open Settings → Automations & scenes → Create automation.
  2. Under When, add Sun → Sunset.
  3. Under Then do, choose Light → Turn on and select your light.
  4. Save it with a name such as “Evening light”.
Create and test in the UI (PT) →

10 / One step at a time

Working well? Add one thing at a time.

These features are optional. You do not need them for your first light with ZHA.

1. Integrations: connect devices

These connect brands and services. ZHA is already an integration. Add others under Settings → Devices & services → Add integration.

2. Apps (Add-ons): extra services

Extra programs installed through the HAOS app store. ZHA does not need MQTT or an extra App. Install one when a specific guide calls for it.

3. HACS: community additions

A community catalog of extra integrations and dashboard elements. It is different from the HAOS app store and may need extra maintenance. Wait until you have a reason to use it.

4. Cameras: start with live view

Check your model’s integration and start with live view in your dashboard. Recording and AI detection come later and have their own requirements.
